cards.title: Build a six-email post-purchase flow with timed emotional beats
cards.summary: Six-email post-purchase sequence timed to the buying window, mixing founder gratitude, upsell, and product education to lift repeat purchases without heavy discounting.
cards.use_when: Setting up or rebuilding the post-purchase email flow for your store (replenishment/retention), especially if you currently only send an order confirmation and shipping notice.
steps: Set the trigger to 'order placed' with no filter so every buyer enters.

Email 1 at 0 minutes: a plain, text-based thank-you from the founder. Split by purchase count (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th+) and change the wording slightly each time (e.g., 'you're almost a VIP' for repeat buyers). Include four things: sincere thanks, mission reminder, support offer, and a P.S. inviting an add-on to the order.
Email 2 at ~24 hours: 'want to add more.' Send a general cross-sell of best sellers or split by product/category for curated recommendations tied to what they bought.
Email 3 at ~3 days: a 'get excited, your order is being handled' message. You don't need a delivery trigger — estimate timing and link products at the bottom.

Email 4 at ~6 days: 'how to get the most out of your product.' Split by what they ordered and give usage tips; add a recommended-product section to pair complementary items. This also reduces returns from misuse.
Email 5 at ~7 days: ask them to follow one social platform (pick a single one, not several).
Email 6 at ~1-2 weeks: a founder check-in asking how the order went, offering support, and optionally a review or repurchase prompt.
After launch, analyze numbers and add or remove emails over time — this is a starting point, not a fixed template.
caveats: Timing past the first day is estimated, not triggered by real delivery data.
The presenter's claimed $48,000 in 30 days is a single case example, not an expected result.
Higher-AOV products may see more buyer's remorse, so the reassurance emails matter more.

cards.title: Exploit the 3-hour post-purchase buyer window
cards.summary: New buyers are far more likely to buy again within hours of ordering, so the first post-purchase email should arrive immediately with an add-on invitation.
cards.use_when: Designing the very first post-purchase email or deciding how aggressive to be with an immediate upsell after checkout.
steps: Send the first post-purchase email within minutes (the presenter's flow uses 0 minutes) rather than waiting a day.
Use the founder gratitude email as the vehicle for the add-on P.S. — it reads genuine rather than pushy, so an add-on invite feels low-pressure.
Reference the extra item the customer may have removed from their cart during checkout; a simple 'you can still add to your order' line is often enough to convert.
Split the message by purchase count so repeat buyers get wording that acknowledges their loyalty, which makes the same add-on ask feel more personal.
Track the placed-order rate of this single email; the presenter reports it converts unusually well for a plain text message.
caveats: The 27% figure for repurchase within the first three hours is cited as third-party research — treat it as directional, not a guaranteed lift for your store.
The presenter notes higher-AOV products carry more buyer's remorse, so push the gratitude/reassurance elements harder than the upsell.

cards.title: Use founder-voice emails to build small-brand trust after purchase
cards.summary: Plain text founder emails outperform designed ones for post-purchase because they read as genuine and reinforce the 'buy from people' feeling.
cards.use_when: Writing the copy and format for post-purchase gratitude and check-in emails where you want authenticity over polish.
steps: Write from the founder personally, using a plain text format with no heavy graphics — even if the customer doesn't buy, the email reads as sincere.
Follow a fixed four-part order: (1) sincere thanks, (2) remind them of the brand mission, (3) offer support if they have questions, (4) encourage a repeat purchase or add-on.
Use subject lines that reflect purchase count: 'your order means the world' (first), 'thank you again' (second), 'third time's a charm' (third), VIP framing (fourth).

For the later check-in, write longer: reference the customer by name, the date of purchase, what results they should expect by now, cite a social-proof number (e.g., '150,000 others'), then offer the chance to shop and to reach out for support.
Expect this check-in to generate useful qualitative feedback because it reads as a personal follow-up.
caveats: The social-proof number must be real — do not invent customer counts or results.
Persona varies: some brands use the actual founder, others a VP or named team member. Keep the voice consistent with who is really writing.

cards.title: Use product-education emails to cut returns and boost repeat orders
cards.summary: Teaching customers how to use what they bought improves their results, which reduces returns and makes them more likely to buy again.
cards.use_when: Writing post-purchase education emails (email 4 in the flow) or building usage guides for products with a learning curve.
steps: Split by what the customer ordered and give tips specific to that product, not generic advice.
Include simple steps to use the product plus tips and tricks — this improves their chance of getting good results, which they will otherwise blame the brand for missing.
Add a recommended-product section that shows how pairing with another product improves results — a subtle cross-sell framed as a benefit, not an ask.
Use subject lines like 'how to get the most,' 'tips and tricks,' or '[Product] 101' to set the expectation of value rather than a sale.
Reuse your strongest campaign content here: if a research or proof email performed well in campaigns, add it to the flow to reaffirm the purchase.
caveats: The presenter notes the recommended-product section is the sales element — keep the email's primary focus on value so it doesn't read as a hard sell.
Also cited as a way to 'stay fresh' by rotating successful campaign emails into flows over time.

cards.title: Set post-purchase email frequency to 3-4 sends per week
cards.summary: The presenter's testing across many frequencies found 3-4 campaigns per week produced the highest revenue with the lowest unsubscribes.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many campaign emails (not flows) to send per week to your list.
steps: Choose a starting cadence of 3-4 campaigns per week — the presenter reports this outperformed both 1-2 per week and 5-7 per week on revenue and unsubscribes.
Avoid 1-2 per week: the presenter says people see ~70 ecommerce brands per day (490 per week), so a weekly send gets forgotten and breaks the habit of opening your emails.
Avoid 5-7 per week: while revenue rises, it plateaus, unsubscribes and complaints climb, and each message's impact is diluted.
Keep every email's weight equal by spreading 3-4 sends across the week rather than clustering.
Ramp gradually, as in the case where a client went from 2x to 4x per week and open rates went from under 50% to 61%.
caveats: These are the presenter's own A/B-tested findings, not a universal rule your list will match — test on your own audience.
The presenter warns that frequency is not the real lever: if you only send sales emails, even 1 per week will annoy your list.

cards.title: Send non-discount content to stay top-of-mind and win repeat purchases
cards.summary: Content that educates and entertains keeps your brand in customers' minds without discounts, priming them to buy when a need arises.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign content for a list you don't want to burn with constant promos, or when trying to protect margins.
steps: Shift campaign content toward value: tips and tricks, founder messages, brand stories, ingredient or product explanations, and 'our favorites' picks.
Avoid relying on discount, buy-or-die, and 'gone forever' style emails — the presenter argues these read as needy and increase sales resistance.
Aim for a healthy balance of product education and product promotion in every campaign calendar.
Think of it as the 'top-of-mind effect': if you appear every other day, when a customer has a random need they think of you first.
Use content to create the 'right place, right time' effect — more sends means more chances a customer happens to be in a buying mood.
caveats: The point is to build a fan base and repeat purchases over time, not immediate sales on every send.
The presenter frames this as protection against rising ad costs and shrinking margins — situational, not a promise.

cards.title: Structure every email around one micro-topic and one takeaway
cards.summary: Each email should cover one small digestible idea using a micro-topic, so the recipient remembers it in the few seconds they open.
cards.use_when: Choosing what each campaign email should say, or when you feel you have 'nothing to send.'
steps: Start from a large macro topic in your industry, product, or niche (e.g., for supplements: building muscle, burning fat, dieting, overall health).
Break each macro topic into many micro-topics — e.g., 'best foods for dieting,' 'how to lower your appetite naturally,' 'best supplements to support dieting,' 'ingredient highlight.'
Write one email per micro-topic and ask: 'What is the one thing I want the customer to know after reading this?'
Use the problem-process-solution framework to structure it: educate on a problem, then the process, then position your product as the solution.
Keep the takeaway to a single point — the presenter argues covering 6 topics means the customer remembers none, while one topic is remembered.
caveats: The 3-5 second open window is the presenter's framing for why short, single-topic emails work.
Micro-topics should still link back to a product benefit so education and positioning work in tandem.

cards.title: Use the problem-process-solution framework to position your product
cards.summary: Educating on a problem and a process primes the reader so that positioning your product as the solution lands naturally as a purchase.
cards.use_when: Writing campaign emails where you want to sell without an explicit discount, or when introducing a product to skeptical buyers.
steps: Educate on the problem first: 'why most people fail at XYZ' or 'why most solutions in this industry are bad.'
Educate on the process: 'how to do XYZ,' 'how to overcome XYZ,' or 'the history / old way of XYZ.'
Present the solution by positioning your product as the answer, then reinforce with how and why it works and how to use it.
Answer the questions your customer is actually asking at each stage so their natural path leads toward the solution (your product).
Use this to earn trust points the buyer needs before making a decision, and to remove friction for the due-diligence they do before buying.
caveats: The presenter stresses subtly positioning the product — the education must be genuinely useful, not a disguised sales pitch.
The framework assumes you can articulate a real problem your product solves.

cards.title: Generate unlimited micro-topics with a ChatGPT prompt
cards.summary: A single well-structured prompt can produce ~100 micro-topic ideas, enough for a year of non-discount campaign emails.
cards.use_when: Building or refreshing your campaign calendar when you need many content ideas quickly.
steps: Define your macro topics first (the big themes in your niche or product), then ask ChatGPT to generate micro-topics under each.
Use a prompt that requests ~100 micro-topic ideas tied to your product and industry, which the presenter says can cover a year of non-discount campaigns.
Review the output and select topics you can genuinely educate on — the presenter notes the best topics come naturally, and AI just gives starting points.
Recycle and refresh topics over time rather than discarding them, since the calendar is meant to keep evolving.
Test the resulting topics against your own knowledge of the niche before sending — AI output is a draft, not final copy.
caveats: The presenter emphasizes AI is 'not perfect' and the strongest ideas come from your own understanding of the market.
The presenter notes the specific prompt and results are available in the free doc — verify the current interface of ChatGPT, which changes.

cards.title: Position email as warm-lead content between cold paid ads and repeat purchases
cards.summary: Email captures attention after paid ads acquire it, then uses cheap content to build trust and drive repeat purchases.
cards.use_when: Deciding which email touchpoints to fund and how email fits with your paid acquisition channels.
steps: Use paid ads (Meta, Google, etc.) for the initial acquisition — getting cold traffic to your site and gaining their attention.
Use email for the later stages: nurture the lead, hold their attention, and drive repeat purchases once they've bought.
Rely on email over paid ads for repeat content because email is cheaper, you own the list, and it's predictable to scale.
Use a pop-up to convert site visitors into subscribers, and plan for a known percentage of subscribers to purchase over time.
Treat email as 'paid ads to people who already know, like, and trust you' — same function of driving traffic, far lower cost.
caveats: The presenter stresses email needs paid ads to grow the list — this is not an argument against paid ads.
Ownership of your list is a key advantage: no third-party platform can shut down your email channel.

cards.title: Understand the trust threshold before asking for a purchase
cards.summary: Customers need multiple exposures to your brand before they trust you enough to buy, so email content exists to accumulate those exposures.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations for email campaign performance with skeptical first-time buyers, or diagnosing low conversion from cold traffic.
steps: Assume most customers have been scammed online and do due diligence before buying — treat trust as the primary barrier, not price.
Recognize the 'trust threshold': the point where a customer trusts you enough to make a purchase (even if they don't need the product yet).
Deliver repeated exposures across multiple channels so that when a customer compares you with a competitor, you're the brand they've seen more often and gotten value from.
Use email as the cheap, repeatable channel to stack those exposures after the first paid touchpoint.
Expect that the customer who has seen you many times and gotten value will choose you over the brand they've only seen three times via paid ads.
caveats: The presenter's comparison (brand seen 8 times across channels vs. 3 times via ads) is a heuristic illustration, not a study result.
The trust threshold isn't measurable in a single number — the presenter describes it as an accumulation over time.

cards.title: Run A/B tests on flows using the flow-level split, not the email-level test
cards.summary: The presenter recommends testing flow emails by adding a conditional split in the flow builder so results are visible without clicking into the email.
cards.use_when: Setting up an A/B test on an email inside a Klaviyo flow and choosing how to build the test.
steps: Add a conditional split to your flow and create a random sample to divide recipients between the two versions.
Copy and paste the original email, edit the copy or design for the variant, then reconnect the flow so both paths continue to the next step.
Use this method rather than the email-level 'create a test' button.
Check results by opening the flow itself — the presenter prefers this because you can see the numbers right when you open the flow without clicking into the individual email.
Review the split's overview numbers to decide which variant to keep.
caveats: This is a tool workflow in Klaviyo; the exact interface and button labels may have changed — verify in your current version.
The presenter prefers this method for visibility and flexibility, but notes it's an opinion, not the only correct approach.

cards.title: Add winning campaign emails into your post-purchase flow
cards.summary: Reuse campaign emails that performed well by inserting them into flows, so proof and education content reinforces the purchase.
cards.use_when: Refreshing an existing post-purchase flow, or when you have a strong campaign email (e.g., a research/proof study) you want more mileage from.
steps: Identify campaign emails with strong performance — the presenter cites research-study or clinical-proof style emails as examples.
Add that email into the post-purchase flow at a point where it reaffirms the purchase (e.g., after the product arrives).
Frame it as reinforcing their decision — 'this is clinically proven' — rather than as a new pitch.
Keep testing by adding and subtracting emails over time rather than setting the flow and forgetting it.
Rotate content so customers in the flow don't see the same messages repeatedly.
caveats: Only reuse emails that actually performed well; a weak campaign email won't improve in the flow.
Any proof claims must be real and compliant — do not fabricate clinical or research claims.

cards.title: Use email frequency to build habitual opens and the exposure effect
cards.summary: Frequent, consistent sends create a habit of opening and leverage familiarity to build loyalty and better open rates.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to send more or less often, or when open rates are declining from infrequent sends.
steps: Send frequently enough (the presenter's tested sweet spot: 3-4 per week) that customers expect and look out for your emails.
Make each email nice to look at and genuinely valuable, so each open delivers a small dopamine hit and they open the next one.
Reinforce the loop: content, engagement, familiarity, loyalty — each cycle strengthens the relationship.
Leverage the exposure effect — people learn to like what becomes familiar, so consistent good content turns subscribers into fans.
Expect open rates from infrequent sending to fall, not rise, because the habit of opening is broken.
caveats: The case mentioned — a client ramping from 2x to 4x per week saw open rates go from high 40s to 61% — is one example and partly reflects better content.
The exposure effect is the presenter's framing; it only works if the content genuinely delivers value.
